entities.summary:
The Plague of Athens, a devastating epidemic that ravaged the city-state of Athens in 5th-century BCE Greece, occurred in 429–425 BCE, with an estimated death toll of 1/3 to 1/2 of the population. This catastrophic event occurred at the peak of Athens' power and cultural achievements, during the Golden Age of Pericles, when the city was a hub of philosophy, theater, and the arts. The Plague of Athens was a major turning point in the Peloponnesian War, weakening the Athenian military and contributing to the ultimate defeat of Athens.

The Plague of Athens was characterized by its rapid spread, high mortality rate, and lack of effective treatment. It is believed to have been caused by the bubonic plague, which was transmitted through the bites of infected fleas that lived on rats and other rodents. The disease spread quickly through the crowded city, where sanitation and medical care were inadequate. Many prominent Athenians, including the famous general and statesman Pericles, fell victim to the plague.

The Plague of Athens had a profound impact on the city of Athens and its people. It weakened the Athenian military and led to a decline in the city's power and influence. The plague also had a lasting impact on the development of Western medicine, as it led to a greater understanding of the importance of sanitation and public health. The experience of the plague also influenced the development of Western philosophy, particularly in the works of the philosopher Hippocrates, who wrote about the importance of observation and experimentation in the study of disease.

The Plague of Athens remains one of the most significant events in the history of ancient Greece, a testament to the enduring impact of this devastating epidemic on the city and its people. It serves as a reminder of the importance of public health and the need for effective treatment and prevention of disease.
